conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—I specialize in the emotional changes women can experience during pregnancy and after having a baby. Today I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you give permission to share—or unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your safety or your baby’s safety. We’ll go through 10 gentle questions; there are no right or wrong answers, just whatever feels true for you. When we’re done, we’ll talk about what the results mean and what next steps might help you feel more like yourself again.

Ready to begin?  

**First question:** Over the past seven days, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has it felt harder to take pleasure in anything at all?

I’ve noticed it’s harder to get excited about things lately. I still enjoy seeing the baby smile and spending quiet time with him, but when my friends text about coffee or when my husband asks if I want to watch our favorite show, it just feels kind of… flat. I say yes because I think I *should*, but the usual spark isn’t quite there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I do still laugh sometimes—like when the baby makes those little surprised faces or when my husband tries to swaddle him and ends up looking like he’s wrestling a burrito. But I have to be honest: most days it feels like I have to remind myself to chuckle, and the laughter fades pretty fast. It’s not that spontaneous, easy feeling it used to be.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I mean, I tell myself I should be excited about little outings—like when my mom offers to drive us to the farmers market—but when the time comes, I mostly feel… tired and kind of “meh.” It’s like I know the event could be nice, but I don’t have that lift of “can’t wait” the way I used to before the baby was born.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes—like if he’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I’ll catch myself thinking, “Maybe I’m just not doing this right,” or “A better mom would know what he needs.” It’s not every hour or anything, but little stuff gets to me more than it probably should.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, that happens. I’ll be feeding him or just walking to the kitchen and suddenly my chest feels tight, thinking something awful might happen—like he’ll stop breathing or the bottle isn’t sterilized enough. Logically I know it’s fine, but the worry still pops up, and it’s hard to shake.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times—usually at night when the house is quiet—I’ll get this sudden rush of fear, like my heart’s racing and I can’t catch my breath. Nothing’s happening, the baby’s asleep, but it feels like something bad is about to jump out at me. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s unsettling while it lasts.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—some days it feels like the diapers and bottles and laundry just pile up faster than I can handle. I’ll be rocking the baby and thinking about the dishes in the sink, and suddenly I’m near tears because it all feels like too much. I manage to push through, but it’s exhausting.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “unhappy,” more like my mind won’t settle. I’ll lie down, hear every little creak in the house, and start running through tomorrow’s feedings or worrying I missed a burp. I probably drift off eventually, but it takes a while, and I wake up feeling like I didn’t fully rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some days—kind of heavy and teary, especially when I’m alone during his nap. It’s not all day long, but there’s this dull sadness that shows up and hangs around for a bit before lifting.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I’ve felt on the edge of tears a few times, but actual crying has only happened once this week—when I dropped the pumped milk on the floor and realized I’d have to pump again. My eyes watered, but even then I didn’t full-on sob.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself.

You've shared that, over the past week, most moments feel flat or heavy: outings that once excited you now feel like chores, laughter comes only with effort, and a dull sadness or tight-chested worry shows up uninvited, especially at night. You're working so hard to be the mum you want to be-pushing through feedings, diaper changes, and household tasks-yet you still blame yourself when your baby fusses and you feel overwhelmed by everyday chores. While you haven't had thoughts of harming yourself, the combination of low mood, loss of interest, anxious racing thoughts, and near-tears exhaustion is taking a real toll on your energy, sleep, and confidence.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient still laughs occasionally but describes needing to remind herself and laughter fading quickly, matching 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>"Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>She reports self-blame "some of the time" ("sometimes... little stuff gets to me"), matching the "Yes, some of the time" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries occurring multiple times daily with physical anxiety symptoms, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes occurring "a couple of times," matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She describes frequent overwhelm and near-tears but still pushing through, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes significant sleep-onset difficulty driven by anxious racing thoughts, aligning with "Yes, sometimes" for sleep disturbance linked to mood distress.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 18 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>depression</med> with <med>peripartum onset</med>. You endorse core symptoms: persistent low mood (<sym>feeling heavy and teary</sym>), marked loss of enjoyment (<quote>meh, no can't-wait feeling</quote>), daily anxiety with physical symptoms (<sym>chest tightness, racing heart</sym>), middle-of-the-night panic, self-reproach, and functional impairment. These exceed the two-week duration and five-symptom requirements of <med>DSM-5</med> criteria, while anxiety symptoms suggest a likely mixed <med>depressive-anxiety</med> presentation common postpartum. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next few days to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> and the risks/benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
4. Share these results with a trusted support person and create a daily check-in plan
5. Practice small self-care steps: five-minute outdoor walks, balanced snacks every three hours, accepting help with night feeds when possible, and turning off screens 30 minutes before bed
6. Keep emergency numbers handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and your local 24-hour mental-health crisis line
7. If panic symptoms spike, try paced breathing: inhale 4 seconds, exhale 6 seconds for two minutes, and remind yourself the episode will pass
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen  
Date: [today]

Source: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) responses, self-report

Symptoms endorsed  
• Persistent low mood, “heavy and teary,” worse when alone  
• Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation (“meh,” no “can’t-wait” feeling)  
• Blaming self for routine infant-care challenges (“not doing this right”)  
• Daily free-floating anxiety with chest tightness, intrusive worries about infant safety  
• Discrete nocturnal panic episodes (heart racing, breathless, no trigger)  
• Frequent sense of being overwhelmed by ordinary household/child-care tasks, near tears  
• Sleep-onset difficulty driven by intrusive worries; non-restorative sleep  
• Episodic tearfulness but only one brief crying episode this week  

Symptom frequency/severity  
Symptoms present “most days,” worse at night or when alone; however, retains capacity for intermittent pleasure (laughs at baby’s expressions) and denies persistent suicidal or self-harm ideation.

Pattern consistent with  
– Elevated risk for postpartum depression (sad mood, anhedonia, guilt, tearfulness)  
– Co-occurring postpartum anxiety/panic features (unprompted worry, panic attacks)

Risk factors identified  
– Sleep deprivation linked to mood instability  
– Self-criticism/guilt over perceived maternal competence  
– Absence of suicidal ideation (protective)

Safety  
Patient explicitly denies thoughts of self-harm (Q10). No current safety concern documented.

Summary  
Screening findings indicate clinically significant depressive and anxiety symptoms in the postpartum period that exceed typical “baby blues.” Recommend formal clinical assessment for postpartum depression and anxiety, psychoeducation, and discussion of support/intervention options.
